title: Over a third of webpages created after ChatGPT's debut show signs of AI writing
content:
Over a third of webpages created after ChatGPT’s debut show signs of AI writing, study finds
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
More than a third of all webpages created after the launch of ChatGPT show signs of AI writing, according to a new study.
The Pew Research Center investigated over half a million English-language webpages from the last five years — finding a sharp rise in machine-written text following the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
Researchers used an AI detection tool called Open Pangram to analyze a random sample of 10,000 webpages collected in July 2026 and found that 10% showed signs of AI authorship, according to the report published last week.
But the share climbed sharply when researchers analyzed only webpages created after ChatGPT’s debut.
More than one-third — 35% — of the post-ChatGPT pages showed signs of AI authorship, echoing other studies suggesting that artificial intelligence is shaping a large part of the modern web.
The trend began after ChatGPT’s launch and accelerated further with the arrival of additional popular chatbots, including Claude and Gemini.
AI-written text still remains far less common on webpages with “.edu” or “.gov” domains and is most commonly found on “.com” pages, the study found.
Though AI detection models are not foolproof, they can expose certain patterns associated with machine-generated writing, including specific punctuation, words, and phrases, researchers said.
The findings come as additional studies revealed that AI chatbots have become increasingly commonplace in Americans’ lives.
A Pew Research Center study released in June revealed that over half of US adults now report using chatbots. Roughly 38% of employed adults also reported using chatbots for work.
Statistics also show that young adults under age 30 are more wary of AI’s potential negative impacts on society than older adults.

report.summary: Over a third of post-ChatGPT webpages show signs of AI writing, per Pew Research study analyzing 500k English-language pages.
report.background: The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 triggered a rapid shift in how online content is produced. The Pew Research Center analyzed over half a million English-language webpages from the last five years, using an AI detection tool called Open Pangram on a random sample of 10,000 pages collected in July 2026. Overall, 10% of all sampled pages showed signs of AI authorship, but among pages created after ChatGPT’s debut, the share jumped to 35%. The rise accelerated as other chatbots like Claude and Gemini gained popularity. AI writing is far less common on .edu and .gov domains, and is most prevalent on .com pages. The study adds to growing evidence that generative AI is now a major force shaping the modern web, while also highlighting that AI detection tools, though imperfect, can identify tells such as unusual punctuation, word choices, and phrasing patterns.
key_points: Pew analyzed 500,000 English-language webpages from the past five years, sampling 10,000 pages in July 2026. They found 10% of all sampled pages showed signs of AI writing, but that figure rose sharply when isolating pages created after ChatGPT launched in late 2022.

Among post-ChatGPT webpages, 35% showed signs of AI authorship. This indicates generative AI tools are now responsible for a substantial portion of new web content, not just a niche experiment or passing trend.

The growth in AI-written text accelerated after additional chatbots like Claude and Gemini entered the market. This suggests that broader availability and competition among AI assistants drove even wider adoption for content creation.

AI-written text is significantly less common on .edu and .gov domains, while .com pages show the highest levels. This points to commercial and entertainment websites as the primary adopters, while academic and government sites remain more cautious or strictly regulated.

AI detection tools like Open Pangram are not foolproof but can identify machine-generated patterns, including specific punctuation, words, and phrases. This highlights an ongoing arms race between AI content generators and tools designed to detect them.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this study confirms that generative AI has become a dominant content-production force on the commercial web, reshaping search engine optimization, publishing, and digital marketing. Developers of detection tools will face growing demand, but also pressure to improve accuracy as AI writing becomes more sophisticated. For regular users, the finding means a large share of the articles, product reviews, and informational pages they encounter may be machine-written, raising questions about trust, originality, and the reliability of online information. It also underscores the importance of media literacy and the need for transparent labeling, while businesses relying on web traffic may need to adapt to search algorithms increasingly designed to filter low-quality automated content.
report.tools: Readers interested in exploring AI-written content detection can watch Open Pangram, the tool used in the Pew study, as well as popular detectors like GPTZero, Originality.ai, and Turnitin. For developers, open-source projects such as GLTR (detecting text generated by LLMs), DetectGPT, and Stanford’s DetectLLM offer hands-on experimentation. Those seeking to understand AI’s influence on the web can also monitor Common Crawl datasets and Pew’s ongoing research on AI adoption.
